title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:

In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. AWS LEARNING CORNER: EXPLORING AWS AMPLIFY & WHY IT’S A GREAT FIT FOR PERSONAL PROJECTS OR STUDENT PROJECTS When working on course projects or personal builds, many of you have likely faced this scenario: you finish the frontend interface quickly, but then spend a disproportionate amount of time setting up the backend, configuring the database, integrating sign-up/login features, and deploying to a server.
To tackle the complexities of infrastructure setup and allow you to focus entirely on application logic, AWS Amplify is a solution well worth considering.
1. What is AWS Amplify? AWS Amplify is a suite of tools and services that enables developers to rapidly build full-stack web and mobile applications on AWS infrastructure, without requiring deep expertise in cloud management or DevOps.
2. Key Features Authentication: Integrate Amazon Cognito using just a few CLI commands or simple configuration steps. It provides built-in workflows for sign-up, sign-in, password recovery, and secure session management. API & Database: Flexibly initialize GraphQL APIs (via AWS AppSync) or REST APIs (using API Gateway combined with DynamoDB). Frontend data operations are optimized and synchronized seamlessly. Hosting & Automated CI/CD: Connect directly to GitHub or GitLab. Whenever new code is pushed (git push), the system automatically handles the build and deployment processes. 3. Real-world Experience Pros:
Rapid Deployment: Ideally suited for demo projects, academic assignments, or MVPs (Minimum Viable Products). Serverless Architecture: Eliminates the cost and effort associated with server maintenance and management. * Multi-platform support: Integrates seamlessly with popular frameworks such as React, Next.js, Vue, Flutter, and React Native. Limitations:
As the application scales and requires deep infrastructure customization (such as configuring custom VPCs or complex IAM permissions), modifying the resources automatically generated by Amplify requires additional research. 4. Conclusion AWS Amplify is an effective solution that streamlines the development process and enables the efficient, standardized deployment of products to the Cloud.

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS LEARNING CORNER: WHAT SHOULD AWS BEGINNERS KEEP IN MIND TO AVOID A “SHOCKING” END-OF-MONTH BILL? A common scenario for those just starting out with AWS is accidentally launching a test resource and forgetting to shut it down—only to be met with an unexpected bill at the end of the month. Learning to control costs not only gives you peace of mind while practicing, but it is also a fundamental skill for managing cloud infrastructure.
Below are some key settings and considerations to help you manage your budget effectively from the very beginning.
1. Setting Up AWS Budgets & Billing Alerts This is the first step you should take immediately after creating an AWS account.
Mechanism: Configure a safe budget threshold (e.g., $5 or $10). If your actual or forecasted costs exceed this limit, the system will automatically send an email notification. Benefit: Prevents resources from running in the background indefinitely without being detected in a timely manner. 2. Making Proper Use of the AWS Free Tier Time Limits: For instance, EC2 offers 750 hours per month for t2.micro or t3.micro instances (depending on the region). If you run two such instances simultaneously, the usage time will be doubled, quickly exceeding the free-tier limit. Capacity Limits: Services like S3 and EBS have specific caps on storage capacity and the number of requests. Be sure to carefully review the service terms before provisioning resources. 3. Cleaning up unused resources “Junk” or orphaned resources are often the source of hidden costs:
Shut down or delete EC2 instances: Stop test servers when they are not in use. Watch out for Elastic IPs: Elastic IPs are only free when associated with an EC2 instance that is in the “Running” state. If an Elastic IP is disassociated or attached to an instance that is in the “Stopped” state, you will still be charged a retention fee. Delete unattached EBS volumes and snapshots: When an EC2 instance is deleted, certain EBS volumes or automatically created snapshots may remain as orphaned resources, continuing to incur storage costs. 4. Detailed Monitoring with AWS Cost Explorer Visualization Tool: AWS Cost Explorer provides charts to analyze costs over time, by service, or by tag. Regular Reviews: Checking your cost reports once or twice a week helps you quickly identify services that are consuming an unusual amount of your budget. 5. Conclusion Cost optimization and control are essential components of the mindset required for working with cloud computing. Establishing a secure infrastructure from the outset allows you to explore and experiment with AWS services with peace of mind, without having to worry about costs.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS LEARNING CORNER: BUILDING A SIMPLE, SECURE STATIC WEBSITE WITH S3 + CLOUDFRONT + ROUTE 53 Once a static website is ready—whether built using plain HTML/CSS/JS or frameworks like React, Vue, or Next.js—the next challenge is choosing a solution for hosting and distributing it over the internet. The typical goals are: cost-efficiency, fast access speeds, secure HTTPS support, and minimal server management overhead.
The trio of Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront, and Route 53 serves as a standardized architecture that addresses these requirements optimally.
1. Solution Architecture & Implementation Steps Step 1: File Storage with Amazon S3
Create an S3 bucket to store the entire set of built static web source files. Configure the S3 bucket policy and grant appropriate access permissions. Enable the “Static website hosting” feature and define default access files (e.g., index.html and 404.html). Step 2: Acceleration & Security with Amazon CloudFront (CDN)
Create a CloudFront distribution and set the previously created S3 bucket as the origin. Acceleration: Web content is cached at edge locations globally, minimizing latency for users. Security: Integrate a free SSL/TLS certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to enable HTTPS. Additionally, configure Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict direct external access to the S3 bucket, ensuring that all traffic must pass through CloudFront. Step 3: Domain Routing with Amazon Route 53
Create a hosted zone for your custom domain in Route 53. Configure an A record (as an alias) to point your domain or subdomain to the CloudFront distribution address. 2. Technical Value & Key Takeaways Cost Optimization: A serverless architecture eliminates the costs associated with maintaining servers (such as Nginx or Apache). For low-traffic scenarios or personal projects, monthly costs are effectively zero. Scalability: The CloudFront CDN network automatically handles sudden spikes in traffic, removing the need for infrastructure upgrades. Simplified Operations: There is no need to worry about patching operating systems or managing SSL certificate renewals. 3. Conclusion This is a classic yet essential exercise that helps you master the mindset of integrating core AWS services to build a complete, secure, and industry-standard system.

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner” Event Objectives Experience a keynote address and fireside chat with Dr. Werner Vogels — Vice President and Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of Amazon. Address a pivotal question regarding the future of the software industry in the AI ​​era: Will artificial intelligence replace software engineers? Gain insights into building large-scale infrastructure, operational excellence, and distributed systems design, drawn from over 20 years of developing Amazon and AWS. Define the profile of the next-generation programmer—the “Renaissance Developer"—equipped to adapt to the wave of Generative AI. Speaker Dr. Werner Vogels - Vice President & Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon. Key Highlights The Million-Dollar Outage & The Birth of Core Technology (DynamoDB) Lessons from an overload incident: Decades ago, during the year’s peak shopping day (December 12), Amazon’s relational database system (RAC) became overloaded and crashed completely for a full day, resulting in millions of dollars in losses. Real-world behavior analysis: Amazon discovered that 70% of data queries were simple Key-Value operations (such as retrieving a shopping cart), 20% involved single tables, and only 10% actually required an RDBMS. Homegrown technology: Relying on off-the-shelf commercial software solutions posed significant risks when operating at hyperscale. This lesson drove Amazon to develop its own proprietary key-value database—the precursor to today’s Dynamo and DynamoDB. 4 Pillars of Operational Excellence Measuring at the 99.9th Percentile (P99.9): Avoid using medians, as they overlook the worst user experiences. Optimization must target the P99.9 level to elevate the entire performance profile. “Everything Fails All the Time” Philosophy: Architect systems to withstand the failure of one or two data centers without service disruption. “GameDays” Culture: Proactively disconnect live production data centers to drill and validate automated failover capabilities and data synchronization. Inverting the IT Economic Model: AWS pioneered the “Pay-as-you-go” model, compelling cloud providers to continuously deliver superior service to retain customers. The Profile of a “Renaissance Developer” To avoid being replaced by AI, developers must cultivate five core qualities:
Curiosity & Eagerness to Learn: Continuous learning is a lifelong commitment, given the ever-changing landscape of languages ​​and frameworks. Systems Thinking: The ability to grasp the big picture of how microservices interact at scale, rather than focusing solely on isolated modules. Ownership: AI can generate code, but humans remain responsible for production bugs, security vulnerabilities, and architectural integrity. T-Shaped Expertise: Deepening expertise in one specific area while maintaining broad knowledge across related domains (UI, business logic, databases). Communication Skills: The ability to distill real-world business problems from trend-driven technical requirements and explain technical trade-offs to stakeholders. AI as a Catalyst – Humans as the Unchanging Core AI accelerates the prototyping cycle from weeks to hours, acting as a “natural language compiler.” However, AI outputs still require human review regarding security, edge cases, and performance. While AI automates repetitive tasks, human judgment, creativity, empathy, and professional pride remain irreplaceable. Key Takeaways Technical & Operational Mindset Look beyond averages: Optimize systems at the P99 or P99.9 level to ensure a positive experience for every customer. Design for failure: Build systems with the assumption that any hardware or network component could fail at any moment. Understand data fundamentals: Analyze data retrieval needs accurately to select the right tool (e.g., Key-Value vs. Relational) and avoid wasting resources. Personal Development Overcoming the fear of AI: AI will not replace humans; however, those who know how to use AI and possess a systems-thinking mindset will replace those who do not. Embracing Admiral Grace Hopper’s quote: “The most dangerous phrase in the language is, ‘We’ve always done it this way.’” Workplace Application Implementing P99.9 Latency: Adjusting the monitoring approach for current projects by focusing on high-percentile metrics. Integrating AI as an Assistant: Leveraging AI to generate boilerplate code and rapid prototypes, while dedicating more time to security reviews, edge cases, and architectural design. Cultivating a T-shaped mindset: Proactively acquiring knowledge regarding the business domain and adjacent technical layers to communicate more effectively with stakeholders. Event Experience Hearing directly from Dr. Werner Vogels—a titan in the fields of cloud computing and distributed systems—was a deeply inspiring experience:
Candor and a practical vision Hearing firsthand the “hard-learned lessons” from Amazon’s multi-million-dollar website outage years ago gave me a profound understanding of the origins of modern cloud services like DynamoDB. Werner’s approach to dispelling fears about AI was compelling: he did not deny AI’s power but positioned it correctly as a supporting tool, emphasizing that true capability lies in architectural mindset and an engineer’s professional integrity. A realistic perspective on software development The session helped move beyond the “just write code” mentality. To advance, an engineer must evolve into a Renaissance Developer—someone capable of bridging the gap between technology and business value.
Key Takeaways Technologies, programming languages, and AI tools will inevitably change over time. The only enduring elements are Systems Thinking, Operational Discipline, and the capacity for continuous self-learning.
Photos from the event Overall, the event not only provided technical knowledge but also helped me reshape my thinking about application design, system modernization, and cross-team collaboration.

title: Introduction
content:
Concepts RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve relevant text first (Retrieval), add it to the prompt (Augmentation), then let the model answer from that text only (Generation). Knowledge base on DynamoDB: legal articles are stored as items in a DynamoDB table and found by keyword. It is simple and fits the AWS Free Tier, but it does not understand meaning the way vector search does. Serverless: Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB scale automatically and charge by usage, which fits a low-budget project. Groq API: an external inference service that runs the language model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b) and is called from Lambda over HTTPS. Problem and goals Employees need fast answers about personal-data rules (for example, using customers’ ID card data for advertising). A public chatbot may invent articles or citations. Goal: answers grounded only in the legal text the team provided, running at near-zero cost on AWS.
Architecture and data flow Architecture and data-flow diagram with numbered steps 1-8
The user opens the website on S3, types a question in the chat box and sends it. index.html sends an HTTPS POST request to API Gateway. API Gateway checks CORS and forwards the payload to the Lambda function. Lambda queries the DynamoDB table LegalArticles for articles related to the question (function retrieve_legal_context). DynamoDB returns the matching articles to Lambda as legal context. Lambda builds a complete prompt (system prompt + legal context + question) and calls the Groq API. Groq returns the generated text answer to Lambda. Lambda formats the standard JSON response (with error codes if needed) and returns it to API Gateway. API Gateway returns the result and the chat box displays it. Lambda logs go to Amazon CloudWatch throughout. Components Component AWS service/resource Prompt & RAG logic Lambda (Python) Knowledge base DynamoDB – LegalArticles Backend API API Gateway + Lambda Frontend S3 static website – index.html Security & operations CloudWatch, Budgets, IAM Implemented vs. planned The system differs from the first design in several places. This table keeps the workshop honest about what exists today.
Area First design Implemented now Knowledge base S3 + Bedrock Knowledge DynamoDB table LegalArticles (keyword lookup) LLM Amazon Bedrock Groq API (external, outside AWS) Frontend AWS Amplify S3 static website Authentication Cognito None yet (public API) Response format Structured: risk level, provisions, evidence… Text answer wrapped in JSON Conversation history DynamoDB Not implemented Incident report + alert SNS Future work AI safety principles Preliminary assessment only, never an official legal conclusion. Answer only from the provided legal articles; never invent provisions or citations. No basis in the database → say so explicitly.

content:
In this section you will create and test an S3 interface endpoint using the simulated on-premises environment deployed as part of this workshop.
Return to the Amazon VPC menu. In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint.
In Create endpoint console:
Name the interface endpoint In Service category, choose aws services In the Search box, type S3 and press Enter. Select the endpoint named com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3. Ensure that the Type column indicates Interface. For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. Make sure to choose “VPC Cloud” and not “VPC On-prem”
Expand Additional settings and ensure that Enable DNS name is not selected (we will use this in the next part of the workshop) Select 2 subnets in the following AZs: us-east-1a and us-east-1b For Security group, choose SGforS3Endpoint: Keep the default policy - full access and click Create endpoint Congratulation on successfully creating S3 interface endpoint. In the next step, we will test the interface endpoint.

title: Test the Gateway Endpoint
content:
Create S3 bucket Navigate to S3 management console In the Bucket console, choose Create bucket In the Create bucket console Name the bucket: choose a name that hasn’t been given to any bucket globally (hint: lab number and your name) Leave other fields as they are (default) Scroll down and choose Create bucket Successfully create S3 bucket. Connect to EC2 with session manager For this workshop, you will use AWS Session Manager to access several EC2 instances. Session Manager is a fully managed AWS Systems Manager capability that allows you to manage your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines (VMs) through an interactive one-click browser-based shell. Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
First Cloud AI Journey Lab for indepth understanding of Session manager.
In the AWS Management Console, start typing Systems Manager in the quick search box and press Enter: From the Systems Manager menu, find Node Management in the left menu and click Session Manager: Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is already running in “VPC Cloud” and will be used to test connectivity to Amazon S3 through the Gateway endpoint you just created (s3-gwe).
Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
You have successfully start a session - connect to the EC2 instance in VPC cloud. In the next step, we will create a S3 bucket and a file in it.
Create a file and upload to s3 bucket Change to the ssm-user’s home directory by typing cd ~ in the CLI Create a new file to use for testing with the command fallocate -l 1G testfile.xyz, which will create a file of 1GB size named “testfile.xyz”. Upload file to S3 bucket with command aws s3 cp testfile.xyz s3://your-bucket-name. Replace your-bucket-name with the name of S3 bucket that you created earlier. You have successfully uploaded the file to your S3 bucket. You can now terminate the session.
Check object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console. Click the name of your s3 bucket In the Bucket console, you will see the file you have uploaded to your S3 bucket Section summary Congratulation on completing access to S3 from VPC. In this section, you created a Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to upload an object. The upload worked because the Gateway endpoint allowed communication to S3, without needing an Internet Gateway attached to “VPC Cloud”. This demonstrates the functionality of the Gateway endpoint as a secure path to S3 without traversing the Public Internet.

title: Proposal
content:
Automated Legal RAG Platform (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP) A Serverless LLM Solution for Real-Time Legal Data Retrieval and Analysis 1. Executive Summary The Automated Legal RAG Platform is designed to assist users and team members in quickly retrieving and analyzing complex legal regulations in Vietnam, specifically focusing on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection. The platform leverages a comprehensive Serverless architecture on AWS combined with a powerful Large Language Model via Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). This solution delivers highly accurate, context-aware queries, eliminating AI hallucination, while minimizing operational costs to nearly $0 by fully utilizing the AWS Free Tier.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Legal documents such as Decree 13/2023/ND-CP are lengthy, dry, and difficult for non-experts to manually navigate and search. Standard general-purpose AI tools (like the free tier of ChatGPT) often lack deep knowledge of Vietnamese law and tend to provide vague answers without an accurate legal basis. Building a self-hosted AI system is typically hardware-intensive and requires complex server management. The Solution Implement an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline: When a user asks a question, the system scans the database to retrieve the most accurate legal clauses and injects them into the System Prompt. The LLM then processes this information to deliver an answer with clear legal citations. Utilize Amazon DynamoDB to store the extracted legal clauses (LegalArticles). Use AWS Lambda for backend RAG logic processing, combined with Amazon API Gateway to provide a stable API Endpoint. Integrate Groq API with the qwen/qwen3.8-27b model for intelligent, coherent natural language generation. Host a static web interface on Amazon S3 Static Website to allow intuitive user interaction via a chat box. Benefits and Return on Investment High Accuracy: Answers strictly follow the provided legal context, ensuring transparency and valid grounding. Cost Optimization: Operates entirely on a Serverless model, maximizing the AWS Free Tier to keep monthly maintenance costs at nearly $0. Scalability: The decoupled architecture allows for the easy addition of new legal frameworks (e.g., Cybersecurity Law, IT Law) to DynamoDB in the future. 3. Solution Architecture The system employs a Serverless architecture, seamlessly connecting the Frontend, Backend, and external LLM.
AWS Services Used Amazon S3 Static Website: Stores and serves the static website interface (index.html, CSS, JS) to users. Amazon API Gateway: Provides a public HTTP/REST API, handles CORS, and acts as the entry point for client requests to Lambda. AWS Lambda (Python): Executes the backend source code to process RAG logic, retrieve data from DynamoDB, and interact with the Groq API. Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles): Stores the structure of legal clauses, supporting high-speed keyword queries. Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b): Synthesizes and analyzes natural language based on the injected legal context. Component Design User Interface (Frontend): Users access the website from S3 and type questions into the chat box. The browser sends an HTTPS POST Request containing the question to the API Gateway. Gateway (API Gateway): Receives the request, checks CORS security headers, and forwards the data payload to the Lambda function. Data Retrieval (DynamoDB): Lambda executes the retrieve_legal_context function to scan and search for relevant clauses in the LegalArticles table (e.g., penalty regulations related to Citizen ID cards and personal data under Decree 13). Augmentation & Generation (Groq API): Lambda packages the user’s question along with the retrieved legal context into a strictly constrained System Prompt (enforcing responses based only on the provided context), then calls the Groq API. Response Flow: Groq returns the result to Lambda, which formats the data into a standard JSON structure and sends it back via API Gateway to be displayed on the user’s chat interface. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Prompt Setup & RAG Mechanism: Build the System Prompt defining the AI’s role as a legal expert and establish Context Constraints to absolutely prevent information fabrication (hallucination). Backend & Database Deployment: Create the DynamoDB table LegalArticles. Write Python code on AWS Lambda integrating data retrieval functions and Groq API calls. Configure API Gateway, enable CORS Headers, and build standardized error handling (returning code 400 for invalid data, 502/504 for system errors, and handling code 429 for Groq API rate limits). Testing & Refinement: Use the curl command to send test HTTP POST requests or test directly on the web interface, and verify logs on Amazon CloudWatch. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Research & Design Phase: Define the legal scope (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP) and design the RAG data flow. Development & Deployment Phase: Build the DynamoDB database, complete the Lambda function, and configure the API Gateway. Integration & Testing Phase: Connect the S3 Static Website frontend with the API Gateway, test the accuracy of answers from the Groq LLM, and optimize error handling. 6. Budget Estimation AWS Infrastructure: Amazon S3: Free (within Free Tier limits). Amazon API Gateway: Free (first 1 million requests/month). AWS Lambda: Free (first 1 million requests/month). Amazon DynamoDB: Free (25GB storage, 25 WCU / 25 RCU). Groq API: Free tier utilized for the open-source model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). Total: 0 USD
7. Risk Assessment API Overload (Rate Limit 429 from Groq API): Mitigation: Implement Error Handling mechanisms and display friendly notification messages on the chat interface when the system temporarily exceeds call frequency limits. AI Hallucination: Mitigation: Tighten the System Prompt with strict rules requiring the use of only the legal context provided by DynamoDB, strictly forbidding external deduction or fabrication. Browser CORS Errors: Mitigation: Fully configure CORS Headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, POST, OPTIONS) directly within the API Gateway settings. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Successfully deploy a complete, auto-scaling, and stable Serverless Backend while optimizing costs to an absolute minimum ($0).
Long-term Value Provide a standardized API endpoint and an intuitive chat interface to quickly and accurately query core regulations within Decree 13/2023/ND-CP, effectively serving academic research and practical study needs.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

AI Legal & Security Assistant Serverless RAG for Legal & Data Protection Compliance on AWS
Overview AI Legal & Security Assistant is a preliminary legal-consultation assistant for businesses, focused on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (personal data protection). Employees type a question or a real scenario; the system looks up relevant legal articles in a database, then a large language model analyzes the question using only those articles.
The system is not a lawyer and does not produce official legal conclusions. If the database lacks a basis, the system must say so.
The system is built on a serverless architecture with these components:
Interface – static web page (index.html) hosted on Amazon S3 static website hosting API – Amazon API Gateway (CORS and standardized errors) Backend – AWS Lambda (Python): retrieves legal articles and calls the LLM Knowledge base – Amazon DynamoDB (table LegalArticles) LLM – Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b), an external service outside AWS Monitoring – Amazon CloudWatch Architecture and data-flow diagram
